title: The Haunted Mansion
full_review:
����������� It's too bad Disney's "The Haunted Mansion" wasn't visited by some ghostwriters, because then maybe the unimaginative fright flick could have scared up some spooky fun, or at least some well-placed audience laughs.

The Eddie Murphy vehicle was inspired (or is that uninspired?) by the eponymous Disneyland ride. And it is Murphy who carries most of the film's (dead) weight. He stars as Jim Evers, an ambitious real estate agent whose workaholic ways have made him miss one too many soccer games, birthday parties and anniversaries.

On the eve of a big family weekend at the lake, he and his wife and business partner, Sara (Marsha Thomason), are summoned by the owner of a huge bayou mansion who wants to sell. Hoping to land the big account, Jim convinces Sara and the kids, Michael (Marc John Jefferies) and Megan (Aree Davis), to make the detour.

What follows is a muddled plot that involves a 19th-century curse, star-crossed lovers and floating ghosts. The only clear thing in director Rob Minkoff's mishmash of a story is that the writers had no idea where to go with it. The special effects are about as good as they are on the ride, which is to say gimmicky and ordinary. Plenty of wispy clouds meant to be netherworld spirits hover about, and at one point Murphy looks into a mirror only to find his face decaying before his eyes.

It takes about half the movie for the Everses to figure out that their gallant hosts, Master Gracey (Nathaniel Parker) and his straight-laced servant Ramsley (Terence Stamp), are ghosts trapped in some kind of limbo. It takes the rest of the film for the family to escape the evil clutches of the rambling Ramsley, who knows more than he lets on.

Thrown in for good Disney measure is a halfhearted attempt at imparting a lesson that family comes first and standing up to one's fears takes guts. But it is such an afterthought that it loses its effect as quickly as the smoky ghosts evaporate.

Also stuck in this amateurish film is a plot thread about Sara resembling Master Gracey's long-lost lover, Elizabeth, who apparently had taken her own life. Gracey thinks Jim's wife is his reincarnated love and can lift the curse by marrying him. The film treads on some dicey territory here with references to suicide, ghosts and the afterlife. None of it is as bad as it reads on the written page, but parents are likely to be troubled by it nonetheless.

All in all, "The Haunted Mansion" is a poor choice for family fare.

Due to some frightening scenes, brief violence and a few instances of crass language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
